chapter: Uniforms, funeral music and horn styles
title: The E-flat clarinet in street bands and talk of finding old instruments
summary: Rene recalls the E-flat clarinet's scream-like sound. The two trade news about current players still using E-flat and C clarinets.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: And you were saying something about the E-flat clarinet coming in there?

Yeah, well, I mean, the E-flat clarinet, the E-flat clarinet used to sound just like a baby scream or something, you know? That little horn. And that used to take plenty of effect. That E-flat clarinet took plenty of effect on people. It would sound just like a child screaming or a person screaming, you know? But that B-flat clarinet don't sound like that, you know? It's all more heavy. But that little E-flat clarinet is no longer there. And boy, they would think it would sound like somebody screaming. And it would sound above the band, you know? Sound above the band. Now they don't use that no more. I've been trying to find the E-flat clarinet, trying to find the C clarinet, but I can't find it. I just want to look at it, just get my eyes on it. That's all I want to do still.
Well, John Casimir still plays E-flat.
Oh, yeah. He's still playing it.
And Paul Bonds has got one.
Well, he just took it up to play with the Eureka.
He just took up the E. He never played E-flat before.
Well, it ought to be hard for him to play an E-flat clarinet.
I know a guy who's got a C clarinet, too.
He don't want to dispose of it, either.
Oh, yeah. He might. I'll give you a song of it if you want. Oh, yeah.
You still looking for a baseball?
